title: API Response Envelope ? Standard Format Across All Routes
text: API Response Envelope ? Standard Format Across All Routes acme API Response Envelope ? Standard Format Across All Routes We decided on a rule: all API endpoints in src/api/routes.ts must always return the standard ApiResponse envelope format: { success: boolean, data?: T, error?: string }. This applies to both successful responses and error responses ? never return a naked object or a bare error string. The envelope makes client-side error handling predictable: clients always check response.success first, then read response.data on success or response.error on failure. It also enables transparent middleware logging and tracing since the envelope structure is consistent. Updated all existing route handlers in src/api/routes.ts to use this envelope and updated the global error handler in src/api/middleware.ts to format thrown errors through the same envelope in production mode (hiding internal details) and development mode (exposing the full error message).

title: Authentication Middleware ? 401 vs 403 Rule
text: Authentication Middleware ? 401 vs 403 Rule acme Authentication Middleware ? 401 vs 403 Rule We established a rule for the authentication middleware in src/api/middleware.ts: always return 401 Unauthorized when the token is missing or invalid, never 403 Forbidden. The HTTP spec is clear: 403 means the server understood the request but the authenticated user lacks permission, while 401 means the request requires authentication or the credentials are invalid. This distinction matters for client-side error handling: a 401 should trigger a redirect to the login page, while a 403 should show an "access denied" UI without redirecting. Mixing them up causes confusing UX where logged-in users are sent back to the login screen when they try to access admin-only routes. Updated src/api/routes.ts to use the authenticate middleware on all protected routes, and added the requireRole factory for role-based access control on admin endpoints.

title: Configuration Rule ? All Secrets via Environment Variables
text: Configuration Rule ? All Secrets via Environment Variables acme Configuration Rule ? All Secrets via Environment Variables We established a rule for src/config.ts: all secrets and credentials must always come from environment variables, never from config files or hardcoded values. The requireEnv helper throws at startup if a required variable is missing rather than falling back to a default ? this prevents silent misconfiguration in production where a missing secret might cause the service to run in a degraded state without anyone noticing. The startup-fail-fast approach is intentional: it is better to refuse to start than to run with missing payment credentials. A failed deployment is visible and recoverable; silent data loss from missing Stripe keys is not. We should also add a secrets rotation runbook for JWT_SECRET and STRIPE_SECRET_KEY ? these should be rotatable without downtime using a dual-key validation window. This is currently not implemented but should be added before GA launch.

title: Database Client ? pg over Prisma for Core Pool
text: Database Client ? pg over Prisma for Core Pool acme Database Client ? pg over Prisma for Core Pool We decided to use the pg (node-postgres) library directly rather than Prisma for the core connection pool in src/db/client.ts. Complex analytics queries in the billing module require raw SQL with window functions and CTEs that do not map well to Prisma's query builder. Prisma is still used exclusively for schema migrations (the declarative schema is valuable for version-controlled migration history), but all runtime queries go through the pg pool. This gives us both migration safety and query flexibility. We chose a max pool size of 20 connections ? this matches our Postgres instance's max_connections divided by 5, leaving headroom for migrations and monitoring connections. Idle timeout set to 30 seconds to prevent stale connections from accumulating under low traffic.

title: Bug: Database Transaction Not Rolling Back on Partial Failure
text: Bug: Database Transaction Not Rolling Back on Partial Failure acme Bug: Database Transaction Not Rolling Back on Partial Failure Discovered a bug where the transaction helper in src/db/client.ts was not correctly calling ROLLBACK when the user callback threw an error. The original implementation used a try/catch but the finally block released the client before the ROLLBACK completed, causing the connection to return to the pool with an open transaction. This crash left the database connection in an inconsistent state where subsequent queries on that connection would receive "ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block" errors. The bug was intermittent and hard to reproduce in development but surfaced under load testing. Fix: restructured the transaction method in src/db/client.ts to always run ROLLBACK before releasing the client in the catch block, and updated src/auth/session.ts to use the transaction wrapper for createSession to ensure the session insert and JWT signing are atomic. Added explicit error logging for ROLLBACK failures (though those are very rare in practice).

title: JWT Library Selection ? jose over jsonwebtoken
text: JWT Library Selection ? jose over jsonwebtoken acme JWT Library Selection ? jose over jsonwebtoken We decided to chose jose over jsonwebtoken for JWT signing because jose is ESM-native and has first-class support for Ed25519 and RS256 algorithms. The jsonwebtoken package predates modern ESM and requires CJS interop shims in our build pipeline. The decision also factored in bundle size: jose is tree-shakeable (only import what you use), whereas jsonwebtoken ships the entire crypto suite even when only HS256 is needed. Updated src/auth/jwt.ts to use the jose SignJWT API and adjusted src/config.ts to expose jwtExpiresInSeconds and refreshTokenExpiresInSeconds as typed config fields.

title: Monetary Amounts ? Always Integer Cents
text: Monetary Amounts ? Always Integer Cents acme Monetary Amounts ? Always Integer Cents We decided on a rule: all monetary amounts must always be stored and transmitted as integer cents (smallest currency unit). Never use floating-point dollar amounts anywhere in the codebase ? not in the database schema, not in API responses, not in internal calculations. Rationale: floating-point arithmetic on currency values causes rounding errors that compound over time. A payment of $9.99 represented as 0.0999 * 100 can produce 9.990000000000001 cents. Using integer cents eliminates this class of bug entirely. The Stripe API itself always returns amounts in cents, so there is no conversion needed at the boundary. Updated src/payments/stripe.ts and src/payments/webhooks.ts to use amountCents variables throughout, and updated src/db/client.ts comments to reflect this convention.

title: Rate Limiting ? Add to Auth Endpoints
text: Rate Limiting ? Add to Auth Endpoints acme Rate Limiting ? Add to Auth Endpoints Idea: we should add rate limiting to the /auth/login endpoint in src/api/middleware.ts to prevent brute-force password attacks. The current implementation has no limit on login attempts per IP, which would allow an attacker to test millions of password combinations against known email addresses. The recommended approach is exponential backoff rate limiting per (IP + email) combination stored in Redis. Using the existing redisCacheUrl connection in src/config.ts, we could use the express-rate-limit package with the rate-limit-redis store. Start with 10 attempts per 15-minute window, doubling the lockout period after each threshold breach. Should also add rate limiting on the /webhooks/stripe endpoint to prevent DoS via fake webhook floods, though in practice Stripe's IP allowlist is a better first line of defense there.

title: Refresh Token Storage ? Switched to Hashed Storage After Security Review
text: Refresh Token Storage ? Switched to Hashed Storage After Security Review acme Refresh Token Storage ? Switched to Hashed Storage After Security Review Fixed a security issue discovered in the session management code in src/auth/session.ts. The original design stored refresh tokens in plaintext in the sessions table. A security review identified this as a problem: if the sessions table is leaked via SQL injection or backup exposure, all refresh tokens would be immediately usable by an attacker. We decided to store only a SHA-256 hash of the refresh token. On validation, we recompute the hash of the incoming token and compare. Production should upgrade this to bcrypt with a cost factor of 10 or higher since SHA-256 is fast enough to brute-force with GPU acceleration. Refresh token rotation was also added: when a refresh token is used, the old session is revoked immediately and a new session is created atomically. This prevents refresh token replay attacks ? if an attacker steals a refresh token and uses it, the legitimate user's next refresh attempt will fail and trigger a security alert.

title: Fixed Token-Refresh Race Condition in session.ts
text: Fixed Token-Refresh Race Condition in session.ts acme Fixed Token-Refresh Race Condition in session.ts Discovered a race condition in the createSession function in src/auth/session.ts. The original implementation generated the session ID after inserting to the DB, causing a window where the signed JWT referred to a session that did not yet exist in the sessions table. Bug reproduction: under high concurrency, a client could receive a valid JWT but immediately get a 401 on their first authenticated request because the session row was not yet committed when the middleware checked it. Fix: now we generate the session ID first using crypto.randomUUID(), then insert the session row, then sign the JWT ? eliminating the race window entirely. The fix also simplifies the control flow since the session ID is available at signing time.

title: Idempotency Keys for Stripe API Calls
text: Idempotency Keys for Stripe API Calls acme Idempotency Keys for Stripe API Calls Idea: we should add idempotency keys to all Stripe API calls that create or modify resources in src/payments/stripe.ts. Stripe supports idempotency keys on POST requests to prevent double-charging when network retries occur. Currently only createSubscription uses an idempotency key. The idempotency key for createSubscription is derived from userId + priceId + date, providing per-day idempotency. This means a customer can safely retry a failed subscription creation within the same day without risk of being charged twice. We should use a similar pattern for any future charge or payment intent creation. Should also evaluate whether to store the idempotency key in our own database to enable cross-service idempotency (not just within Stripe's 24-hour window). This would matter if we ever replay failed operations from a message queue.

title: Payment Provider Decision ? Stripe over Paddle
text: Payment Provider Decision ? Stripe over Paddle acme Payment Provider Decision ? Stripe over Paddle We decided to chose Stripe over Paddle as our payment processor. Key factors: Stripe has a more mature webhook reliability story with configurable retry policies, event logging in the dashboard, and signature verification. Paddle's merchant-of-record model would have simplified EU VAT compliance but removes control over checkout UX customization. Our team also had existing Stripe integrations from previous projects, reducing onboarding time. The Stripe TypeScript SDK is well-maintained and ESM-compatible, matching our stack. Updated src/payments/stripe.ts to wire the Stripe SDK and updated src/config.ts to add stripeSecretKey and stripeWebhookSecret as required environment variables.

title: Subscription Cancellation ? Graceful by Default
text: Subscription Cancellation ? Graceful by Default acme Subscription Cancellation ? Graceful by Default We decided that subscription cancellation should default to cancel_at_period_end rather than immediate cancellation. Users who cancel should retain access until the end of the period they have already paid for ? this is both fair to customers and reduces churn-related support requests. Immediate cancellation is reserved for admin actions (e.g., fraud or TOS violations) and requires the admin role to invoke via the DELETE /subscriptions/:id?immediate=true endpoint. Updated src/payments/stripe.ts and src/api/routes.ts to enforce this role check. Should also add a cancellation confirmation email that clearly states when access will expire. This is currently a TODO in the handleInvoicePaymentFailed handler ? the dunning email workflow is not yet wired up.

title: Security Fix ? Prevent User Enumeration on Login Endpoint
text: Security Fix ? Prevent User Enumeration on Login Endpoint acme Security Fix ? Prevent User Enumeration on Login Endpoint Fixed a user enumeration vulnerability in the POST /auth/login handler in src/api/routes.ts. The original implementation returned 404 Not Found when the email did not exist in the database, which allowed an attacker to enumerate valid email addresses by observing whether the response was 404 (email not found) or 401 (wrong password). Fix: both cases now return 401 Unauthorized with the same generic message "Invalid credentials". The timing of the response is also equalized ? even when the user is not found, we still perform a dummy bcrypt comparison to prevent timing side-channel attacks where a fast 404 response reveals that the email does not exist. This fix follows the OWASP guidance on preventing user enumeration at authentication endpoints. Combined with the rate limiting we should add to the middleware, this significantly hardens the login endpoint against automated attacks.

title: Webhook Idempotency ? Processed Events Table
text: Webhook Idempotency ? Processed Events Table acme Webhook Idempotency ? Processed Events Table Idea: we should add idempotency handling to the Stripe webhook processor in src/payments/webhooks.ts to prevent double-processing of events when Stripe retries failed deliveries. Stripe can retry a webhook event up to 72 hours after the first attempt. Implemented a processed_webhook_events table approach: before processing any event, we INSERT the event ID into the table. If the event is already recorded, we return 200 immediately and skip business logic. This is more reliable than checking for side-effects because some operations (like creating a payment record) are not idempotent by nature. We should also improve the error recovery path: currently, if business logic throws after recording the event, the event is marked failed but never retried internally. Should add a dead-letter queue or manual retry mechanism for failed webhook events.

title: Bug: Webhook Signature Verification Failing on Express with Body Parser
text: Bug: Webhook Signature Verification Failing on Express with Body Parser acme Bug: Webhook Signature Verification Failing on Express with Body Parser Bug reproduction: the handleStripeWebhook function in src/payments/webhooks.ts was receiving a parsed JSON object instead of the raw Buffer. Stripe's stripe.webhooks.constructEvent requires the exact raw bytes of the request body to compute the HMAC-SHA256 signature. The issue was in the Express app setup ? express.json() middleware was applied globally, including to the /webhooks/stripe route, which parsed the body before our webhook handler could access it as a Buffer. This broke signature verification with the error "No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload". Fix: registered express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }) specifically for the /webhooks/stripe route before the global json middleware, and updated src/api/routes.ts to document that req.body must be a raw Buffer for this endpoint. Verified the fix with a Stripe CLI webhook replay.

title: Acme SaaS Backend ? Project Kickoff
text: Acme SaaS Backend ? Project Kickoff acme Acme SaaS Backend ? Project Kickoff Initialized the Acme SaaS backend repository. We decided on a modular TypeScript architecture with separate modules for auth, payments, and API. This structure allows independent testing and deployment of each subsystem. Set up the project structure: src/auth/, src/payments/, src/db/, src/api/, and src/config.ts. Each module owns its domain logic and exposes a clean TypeScript interface to other modules.
